title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
seo_title: Mechanical Properties of Fluids Class 11 Physics Worksheet with Answers (NCERT Chapter 9)
standard_code: Class 11 Physics, Chapter 9: Mechanical Properties of Fluids
standard_text: Pressure due to a fluid column, Pascal's law and its applications (hydraulic lift and hydraulic brakes), effect of gravity on fluid pressure, viscosity, Stokes' law, terminal velocity, streamline and turbulent flow, critical velocity, Bernoulli's theorem and its simple applications, surface energy and surface tension, angle of contact, excess of pressure across a curved surface, application of surface tension ideas to drops, bubbles and capillary rise.

body_html:
How to think about it

Pressure in a liquid at depth h is ρgh above the surface pressure. Pascal's law lets a hydraulic lift multiply force: F₂ = F₁A₂/A₁. In steady flow A₁v₁ = A₂v₂, so liquid speeds up in a narrow pipe; Bernoulli's principle says the pressure there is lower.

Viscosity is fluid friction; a small sphere reaches terminal velocity v = 2r²(ρ − σ)g/9η (Stokes' law). Surface tension pulls drops into spheres; the excess pressure is 2T/r in a drop and 4T/r in a bubble, and water rises h = 2T cos θ/(rρg) in a capillary.

Example

10 m of water. Pressure?

1000 × 9.8 × 10

Answer: 98,000 Pa

Example

F₁ = 100 N, A₂/A₁ = 100. F₂?

100 × 100

Answer: 10,000 N

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the 2 in 2T/r for a drop.
  • Thinking pressure is higher where flow is faster.
  • Leaving cm² unconverted in Pascal's law (only the ratio matters).

faq.a: Along a streamline p + ½ρv² + ρgh is constant, so where a fluid flows faster its pressure is lower.

faq.q: Why does water rise in a thin glass tube?
faq.a: Surface tension and adhesion to glass pull it up: h = 2T cos θ/(rρg).
